text: Metadata Management & Business Glossary gave you the vocabulary and the inventory — what a column is called, what it means, who owns it, and where it lives in the catalog. This course goes deep on the next layer: lineage, the recorded path data takes from where it originates to everywhere it ends up, through every transformation along the way.

A plain definition — 'tracking where data comes from' — is accurate but incomplete; it misses the every-transformation part, where most real problems hide. The sharper version: lineage lets you answer, step by step, exactly how a number got to be the number you're looking at, and exactly what else would be affected if any step in that chain changed. A revenue figure on a dashboard didn't appear from nowhere.

A shipped package gets scanned at every stage — pickup at the warehouse, a sorting facility, a truck, delivery. The tracking page isn't the package, it's the recorded path it took, hop by hop. Data lineage does the same job: a source system, an extraction job, a transformation step, a warehouse load, a semantic model, a dashboard. Each arrow is a hop — the lineage equivalent of a package scan. If a number looks wrong, you don't guess; you walk the hops backward until you find where it diverged.

You already use lineage thinking. A bank wire's trail — sent from one account, cleared through an intermediary, deposited to another — lets anyone retrace exactly how funds moved. A document's version history, like Track Changes in Word or Google Docs' revision history, records who changed a paragraph, when, and what it looked like before. A food label's sourcing trail — grown in one region, processed at one facility, packaged at another — is farm-to-table lineage.

Two terms worth locking in now. A hop is one recorded step in a data's path — an extraction, a transformation, or a load. A source system is where a piece of data originates, before any lineage hop has happened to it. Together they're the vocabulary the rest of this course builds on: every lineage record is just a chain of hops starting from a source system.

Over this course's five chapters, you'll go from these core concepts, to tracing data through real system types, to using lineage for impact analysis, to documenting it, and finally to applying all of it in realistic scenarios. Next lesson: why lineage matters, and what actually breaks without it.
